full_report.executive_summary: The recorded actions show an 11-year-old winger who uses close touches, turns and body feints to advance the ball. His passing stands out, with three verified passes leading to teammate goals. He also takes two recorded shots himself: one is saved and one scores after his own dribble. Keeping possession through crowded challenges is a useful development focus, with both a successful carry through contact and a recorded loss while shielding. These are promising attacking examples, but the partial observation packet cannot establish his full-match level or long-term potential.

exercises.name: Protect and escape
exercises.description: In a small square, protect the ball from a partner using light pressure. Turn through an open gate when space appears, keeping the ball within reach.

exercises.name: One defender, two gates
exercises.description: Attack two gates against one defender with close touches and a change of direction. Reset after each attempt and discuss which exit was available.

exercises.name: Carry or release
exercises.description: Play two attackers against one defender toward a small goal. The ball carrier chooses to continue or pass as the defender commits.

exercises.name: Final touch and finish
exercises.description: Dribble around a marker and take a final touch into a comfortable shooting position. Aim at a chosen part of the goal rather than simply striking harder.

exercises.name: Next-action game
exercises.description: Play a short three-against-three game with normal scoring. After losing the ball, reward a useful recovery action such as closing the carrier or covering a pass.

training_plan.ninety_day_plan: Progress to crowded small-sided games and compare full-match examples of shielding, releasing and finishing with the starting observations.

Keep home practice short and let him choose between two games.
Ask what he noticed when a defender came close rather than telling him every answer.
Use full-match observations with his coach before drawing conclusions about level or ability.

Turn and carry through the gate when the route opens.

home_drills.equipment: A ball, two markers and a partner
steps: Place the markers as a passing gate.
Take a few close touches before passing through it to a partner.
Change the approach angle and try again.
home_drills.success_sign: The partner receives a controlled pass after the dribble.

home_drills.name: Touch then target
home_drills.equipment: A ball and a safe target
steps: Choose a small target in a safe playing area.
Dribble toward it and set the ball with a final touch.
Finish gently toward the target and repeat from another angle.
home_drills.success_sign: The final touch leaves him ready to aim without stretching for the ball.

lessons.what_scouts_look_for: Coaches watch whether a player keeps the ball within reach while a defender challenges. They also look for a useful exit touch or release.
lessons.why_it_matters: At 11, close control needs practice against realistic but manageable pressure. Keeping the ball secure gives a winger more chances to use a pass or dribble.
lessons.what_happened: The player's first name was not supplied. At 00:08.883, his shielding sequence ends in a loss. At 00:27.882, he keeps going through a close challenge. These contrasting examples make protection a useful practice target rather than an established general weakness.
lessons.personal_advice: Practise protecting against light pressure before turning through one of two gates. Add a teammate so you can also choose a short release instead of always escaping alone.
lessons.age_benchmark: The mixed challenge outcomes support a cautious lower strong-club indication for a U11-U12 winger, not a measured peer ranking.
lessons.simple_explanation: Protecting the ball is like keeping a toy within reach when someone tries to take it. The next step is finding a clear way out rather than staying trapped.

moments.what: He releases a short ball through a crowded challenge for a teammate to finish directly.
He passes low across the advancing goalkeeper for a teammate's close-range finish.

lessons.what_scouts_look_for: Coaches watch how a player chooses between carrying, passing and shooting. A useful choice fits the available space and the defender's action.
lessons.why_it_matters: Young wingers benefit from learning that carrying and passing work together. At this age, simple games with choices are more useful than prescribing the same move every time.
lessons.what_happened: The player's first name was not supplied. At 00:49.615, he releases through a crowded challenge. At 00:56.264, he sends the ball across the goalkeeper. Both finishes belong to teammates, while his contribution is the pass.
lessons.personal_advice: Play two attackers against one defender and choose whether to carry or release. Talk briefly about which option was open rather than judging only whether a goal followed.
lessons.age_benchmark: These attacking choices support the supplied 7/10 decision-making grade within the U11-U12 pro-academy guide range, without establishing overall academy readiness.
lessons.simple_explanation: Choosing a pass is like choosing the clearest route through a busy room. Sometimes moving yourself helps, and sometimes giving the ball to someone with more room works better.

moments.what: After the shielding loss, he gets up and chases the recovering opponent to challenge again.

lessons.what_scouts_look_for: Coaches watch the next useful action after possession is lost. That might be closing the carrier or covering a nearby option.
lessons.why_it_matters: Mistakes are normal at 11. Practising a simple next action helps a child stay involved without dwelling on the outcome.
lessons.what_happened: The player's first name was not supplied. He loses possession in the shielding sequence. At 00:12.633, he gets up and closes enough to challenge again. This is one positive response, not proof of a general mental trait.
lessons.personal_advice: In small-sided games, practise choosing one useful recovery action after a loss. Praise the action rather than demanding that every chase wins the ball.
lessons.age_benchmark: This is a constructive U11-U12 recovery example, although one sequence cannot establish a consistent habit.
lessons.simple_explanation: It is like dropping something during a game and immediately helping put things right. The important part is doing something useful next, not pretending the mistake never happened.

homework_plan.why: This repeats the next-action habit shown at 00:12.633 without requiring a win every time.

parent_corner.size_and_potential: Your child's first name and physical measurements were not supplied, so neither identity details nor size-based conclusions are added here. The useful evidence concerns his football actions. At 00:44.015, he passes through a defensive gap for a teammate to finish. Value that skill without comparing bodies or predicting adult potential.
parent_corner.development_takes_time: Your child already has useful close-control and passing examples to build on. Protection under pressure is the clearest next practice theme. A lost ball in one sequence and a successful carry in another show why repeated observation matters. Look for gradual improvement across months rather than expecting every challenge to end well.
parent_corner.your_role_on_the_sideline: At 00:12.633, he responds to a loss by chasing to challenge again. Praise that useful next action without shouting a stream of instructions. Let his coach guide the football decisions and ask him afterwards which moments he enjoyed.
parent_corner.how_to_support_mentally: The packet shows his recovery chase at 00:12.633, but it does not tell us how he felt. Avoid assuming frustration, confidence or disappointment.
